name: GLOW
used_for: Marketed by research-peptide sellers and clinics as a skin, collagen, hair and soft-tissue repair blend. These uses are promotional claims, not approved indications.
summary: GLOW is a nickname for a three-peptide blend of GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500. No approved product contains it, and no combination-specific human study was found in the sources reviewed. A Florida wellness clinic's guide describes such blends as not standardized products and says a blend does not automatically have clinical evidence because its ingredients were researched separately. The detailed information is on the pages for GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500; formulations vary by seller. The combination's side effects are not separately characterized.

administration_guidance.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site (which carries supplier affiliate links) warns against combining separate-vial peptides in one syringe because of differing stability and pH needs, and says reconstituted solutions are refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees C, with TB-500 having the shortest stability window of 1 to 2 weeks and BPC-157 and GHK-Cu up to 30 days.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site (which carries supplier affiliate links) lists injection-site irritation, short-term fatigue and occasional headache, and states the blend is not FDA-approved.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site says the name GLOW comes from the GHK-Cu component and associates the blend with soft-tissue repair, skin and collagen remodeling, anti-inflammatory effects and hair density.
A Florida wellness clinic's guide describes GLOW as a peptide blend rather than a standardized product and notes that human research on BPC-157 remains extremely limited.

dose.summary: Sellers describe a pre-mixed 70 mg vial with GHK-Cu, TB-500 and BPC-157 in roughly a 5 to 1 to 1 ratio, and a daily dose of about 2 to 2.8 mg of blend. No study has tested any dose of this combination, and formulations vary by seller.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, describes a 70 mg vial of 50 mg GHK-Cu, 10 mg TB-500 and 10 mg BPC-157 (a 5 to 1 to 1 ratio). It says 10 units (0.10 mL) after adding 3 mL of bacteriostatic water gives about 1.67 mg GHK-Cu, 0.33 mg TB-500 and 0.33 mg BPC-157.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer, an education site that says it does not sell peptides, describes a 5 to 1 to 1 ratio (GHK-Cu to BPC-157 to TB-500) and 2,000 to 2,500 mcg of total blend injected under the skin once daily.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to a seller, describes 2.8 mg per injection (about 2 mg GHK-Cu, 400 mcg BPC-157 and 400 mcg TB-500) from 70 mg or 90 mg freeze-dried vials, and says formulations are sold in different sizes.
items.label: internet

timing.summary: The only timing advice found is that morning or evening both work. No study has tested timing for this combination.

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says to inject in the morning or evening and that consistency matters more than the hour.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: Online sources describe one injection a day, either 5 to 7 days a week or Monday to Friday. One site describes the TB-500 part as twice weekly when the peptides are bought as separate vials. None of this has been studied.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols says the pre-blended vial is a once-daily injection under the skin. For separate vials it lists BPC-157 and GHK-Cu daily and TB-500 twice a week.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer describes one injection a day, 5 to 7 days per week, during the active cycle.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind describes 5 days per week, Monday through Friday, for 7 weeks focused on skin and hair.
items.label: internet

cycle_length.summary: Online sources describe 4 to 6 weeks on and 2 to 4 weeks off, with longer cycles of 8 to 12 weeks on and 4 to 8 weeks off. These come from sellers and guides, not from combination studies.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols describes 4 to 6 weeks on and 2 to 4 weeks off as standard and 8 to 12 weeks on with 4 to 8 weeks off as extended. It says GHK-Cu typically sets the cycle length because of copper-handling considerations.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer describes 4 weeks on and 2 to 4 weeks off as the standard cycle.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind describes about 4 to 6 weeks on and 2 to 4 weeks off, with some extended protocols of 8 to 12 weeks on and 4 to 8 weeks off.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: Sources disagree on mixing: one says never to combine separate vials in one syringe, another allows drawing each into one syringe just before injecting but not storing a DIY mix. Reconstituted vials are kept refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees C for about 28 to 30 days, with TB-500 the shortest. No stability study of the blend was found.

items.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site (which carries supplier affiliate links) warns against combining separate-vial peptides in one syringe because of differing stability and pH needs.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site (which carries supplier affiliate links) says reconstituted solutions are refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees C, with TB-500 having the shortest stability window of 1 to 2 weeks and BPC-157 and GHK-Cu up to 30 days. These windows describe the separate components.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols says the dry powder is kept at -20 degrees C long term and that the 70 mg pre-blend vial is reconstituted with 3.0 mL of bacteriostatic water, giving about 23.3 mg/mL.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says each peptide can be drawn into the same syringe and injected once, but not pre-mixed into a storage vial because long-term stability of the DIY mix has not been tested. It says to store at 2 to 8 degrees C, protected from light, and use within 28 days.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind says the powder is frozen for long-term storage, or refrigerated for up to four weeks. After mixing it says to refrigerate, protect from light and use within about a month. For separate vials it says each is injected with its own syringe rather than mixed together. It names the abdomen or thigh as injection sites.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: Sellers and guides describe the blend as three peptides with complementary roles: blood vessel growth, cell movement and collagen remodeling. This is the sources' description, not a tested mechanism of the combination.

items.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site says the name GLOW comes from the GHK-Cu component and associates the blend with soft-tissue repair, skin and collagen remodeling, anti-inflammatory effects and hair density.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols describes three roles: BPC-157 for blood vessel growth and tissue protection, TB-500 for actin (a protein that helps cells move), and GHK-Cu for collagen, elastin and skin remodeling.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says BPC-157 builds new blood vessels, TB-500 mobilizes repair cells and GHK-Cu provides copper to cross-link collagen.
items.label: internet

best_documented_effect.summary: No human trial or registered study of GLOW or of these three peptides together was found. Sources state this themselves, so there is no documented effect of the combination.

items.text: A Florida wellness clinic's guide describes GLOW as a peptide blend rather than a standardized product and notes that human research on BPC-157 remains extremely limited. The BPC-157 point describes that one component.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols says no published human trial has tested BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu together and that the combination is built from research on the individual compounds.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says no human clinical trials exist for this specific three-peptide blend.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind says no published human trial has evaluated the three compounds together as a fixed combination.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: Sellers and guides list injection-site irritation, short-term fatigue and occasional headache. These are not from combination studies.

items.text: The Peptide Dosing Protocols site (which carries supplier affiliate links) lists injection-site irritation, short-term fatigue and occasional headache, and states the blend is not FDA-approved.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer lists mild injection-site redness and transient fatigue as common, and nausea, dizziness and a temporary flare of old injuries as uncommon.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind lists mild injection-site irritation (redness, itching or soreness), short-term fatigue and occasional headache.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Warnings
side_effect_groups.summary: One site says the main concern with the stack is overlapping blood-vessel-growth signaling, so people with active cancer or retinal vascular disease are told to avoid it. This is a seller-side warning, not a study result.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols names overlap of blood-vessel-growth signaling from BPC-157 and TB-500 as the main stack concern. It lists active cancer or a strong cancer history and active retinal vascular disease as contraindications.
items.label: internet
